unit-m4u4.title: Unit 4 · Lesson 4: Multiply a Decimal by a Whole Number
unit-m4u4.source: enVision Topic 4 Student Edition practice pages — multiplying decimals (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 4-4 practice pages: multiplying a decimal by a whole number by multiplying as whole numbers and placing the point, using number sense to place it, telling which equation is not true, and word problems about money, weight and area.

why.text: This is the lesson the unit has been building to: the rule she will use every time a decimal and a whole number are multiplied.

objectives.text: Multiply a decimal by a whole number and place the decimal point
Use number sense or counting places to place the point
Explain why a product can show fewer decimal places than the factor
Solve word problems that multiply a decimal by a whole number

parentNote.text: Built from the lesson 4-4 practice pages in her Unit 4 folder, read for what they ask. The numbers are fresh, not the page's own. Every wrong option on a worked product comes from a named slip: the point left out, the point one place too far either way, or the zero in a whole number like 40 dropped before multiplying. One question answers the page's own puzzle about a product with fewer decimal places (0.45 × 6 = 2.70 = 2.7). Her class teaches this unit after Unit 5.

nextUp.text: Multiply as whole numbers, count the places, place the point, then check with an estimate.

cards.def:
**Multiply as if there were no decimal point, then put the point in the product.**
• 0.15 × 12 → 15 × 12 = 180 → 1.80.

**The product has as many decimal places as the factors have together.**
• 0.36 has 2 and 14 has 0, so 0.36 × 14 = 5.04 has 2.
**Estimate to place the point: 4.7 × 6 is about 5 × 6 = 30, so 28.2.**

**A zero between digits is a real digit; keep it.**
• 0.58 × 7 = 4.06, not 4.6.

**After placing the point you may drop zeros at the end: 2.70 is 2.7.**
• So a two-place decimal times a whole number can show one place.

**Multiply by the whole number exactly as written, zeros and all.**
• 7.25 × 40 = 290, not 29.
cards.hint: A zero in 40 is part of the number.

cards.def:
**If one factor is 10 times bigger and the other 10 times smaller, the product stays the same.**
• 0.6 × 48 = 6 × 4.8 = 60 × 0.48 = 28.8.

**Estimate before or after: if the answer is about 10 times too big or small, move the point.**
• $0.35 × 64 is about $21, so $22.40 fits.

questions.q: What are the two steps to multiply a decimal by a whole number?
opts: Multiply as if there were no decimal point, then place the point
Line up the decimal points, then add the numbers
Round both numbers, then write the rounded product
Drop the decimal point, and leave it out of the answer
steps: Multiply the digits as whole numbers.
Count the decimal places in the decimal factor.
Give the product the same number of places.

ex.main: **Multiply as whole numbers, then place the point.** Rounding is for estimating, not for the exact answer.

questions.q: For 0.36 × 14, how many decimal places does the product have before you drop any zeros?
opts: One, because 14 has no decimal
Two, the same as 0.36
Three, two plus one more for 14
None, because 14 is a whole number
questions.hint: Count the digits after the point in each factor.

ex.main: **Two.** The places in the factors add up: 2 from 0.36 and 0 from 14. 0.36 × 14 = 5.04.
ex.tip: Count the places in the factors.

questions.q: What is the same about 24 × 13 and 2.4 × 13?
opts: Both products are 312, exactly the same number
Nothing; a decimal product always has different digits
The digits of the product, 312; only the point is in a different place
Both products have one decimal place, like 2.4

ex.main: **The digits, 312.** 24 × 13 = 312 and 2.4 × 13 = 31.2. Only the point moves.
ex.tip: Same digits; the point tells the size.

steps: Of 28.2, 2.82, 282 and 0.282, only 28.2 is close to 30.

ex.main: **28.2.** 4.7 × 6 should be close to 5 × 6 = 30, and 28.2 is.
ex.tip: An estimate tells you where the point goes.

questions.hint: Check where the point goes in each product.
steps: 6.4 × 3 has one decimal place, so it is 19.2, not 1.92.

ex.main: **6.4 × 3 = 1.92.** 6.4 has one decimal place, so the product does too: 19.2. The other three are true.
ex.tip: Count the places in the factors; the product has the same.

questions.hint: 58 × 7 first. Watch for a zero in the answer.
steps: 0.58 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 4.06.
Check with an estimate: 0.6 × 7 = 4.2, close to 4.06.

ex.main: **4.06.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 406 is the decimal point left out; 40.6 is the point one place too far right; 0.406 is the point one place too far left.
ex.tip: A zero inside 4.06 is a real digit; keep it.

steps: 3.4 has 1 decimal place, so the product has 1: 88.4.
Check with an estimate: 3 × 26 = 78, close to 88.4.

ex.main: **88.4.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 884 is the decimal point left out; 8.84 is the point one place too far left; 29.4 is adding instead of multiplying.

steps: 0.47 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 7.52.
Check with an estimate: 0.5 × 16 = 8, close to 7.52.

ex.main: **7.52.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 752 is the decimal point left out; 75.2 is the point one place too far right; 0.752 is the point one place too far left.

steps: 0.006 has 3 decimal places, so the product has 3: 0.312.

ex.main: **0.312.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 312 is the decimal point left out; 3.12 is the point one place too far right; 0.0312 is the point one place too far left.
ex.tip: Three places: write a zero after the point if you need one.

steps: 7.25 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 290.00.
Check with an estimate: 7 × 40 = 280, close to 290.

ex.main: **290.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 29 is the zero in the whole number dropped before multiplying; 2,900 is the point one place too far right; 29,000 is the decimal point left out.
ex.tip: Keep the zero in 40 when you multiply.

questions.q: Ivy multiplies a whole number by a decimal with two decimal places. She says the product could have only one decimal place. Is she right?
opts: No: the product must have three places, two plus one
No: the product must always have exactly two places
Yes: 0.45 × 6 = 2.70, which is the same as 2.7
Yes, but only if the whole number is 1
questions.hint: What happens when a product ends in 0?
steps: A zero at the end does not change the value, so 2.70 = 2.7.

ex.main: **Yes.** 0.45 × 6 = 2.70, and 2.70 is 2.7. When the product ends in zero, it can be written with fewer places.
ex.tip: Count places first, then drop end zeros.

questions.q: A bakery makes $0.35 on each muffin it sells. It sells 64 muffins. How much does it make?
steps: Check: 0.35 is about a third, and a third of 64 is about 21.

ex.main: **$22.40.** 35 × 64 = 2,240, and two places makes 22.40. The other amounts put the point in the wrong place.

questions.q: A backpack may weigh at most 25 pounds. It holds two books of 6.8 pounds each and a lunchbox of 9.5 pounds. Is it within the limit?
opts: Yes: 6.8 + 9.5 = 16.3 pounds
questions.hint: Find the weight of the two books first.

ex.main: **Yes: 23.1 pounds.** 32.6 counts the lunchbox twice, 16.3 leaves a book out, and 231 drops the decimal points.
ex.tip: Count each thing once, then compare.

questions.q: A rectangle is 3.5 meters wide. Its length is a one-digit whole number of meters. What are its least and greatest possible areas?
opts: 0 and 31.5 square meters
3.5 and 31.5 square meters
3.5 and 35 square meters
35 and 315 square meters
questions.hint: The smallest one-digit length is 1, and the largest is 9.

ex.main: **3.5 and 31.5 square meters.** A length of 0 is not a rectangle, 10 is not one digit, and 35 and 315 drop the decimal point.
ex.tip: One-digit whole numbers run from 1 to 9.

opts: 0.6 × 48 is the least
60 × 0.48 is the greatest
All three equal 28.8
6 × 4.8 is the greatest
questions.hint: Each one is 6 × 48 = 288 with the point placed somewhere.

ex.main: **All three equal 28.8.** One factor got 10 times bigger while the other got 10 times smaller, so the product stayed the same.
ex.tip: Ten times bigger and ten times smaller cancel out.
